title: Institutions and Investments
abstract: As China continues to be heralded as a rising economic power, the need for an understanding of its institutional effects--such as investment-related policies, regulations, and laws--on foreign direct investment increases as well. Institutions and Investments employs interdisciplinary perspectives from economics, business, law, and political science to shed light on the interaction between institutional changes and investment patterns and to form a clear picture of investment behavior as China's legal and regulatory infrastructure has developed over the reform years. Organized into three main parts, the book first discusses the evolution and nature of China's FDI regulatory framework. Part 2 examines the various modes and variant patterns of FDI in China in the reform years. Part 3's central task is to demonstrate a systematic link between institutional changes in China's FDI regulatory framework and the changing patterns of FDI. In conclusion, Jun Fu finds that China has made substantial progress from a command economy to a market system, but that it still has a long way to go before it truly attains a transparent and rule-based system. This book adds new dimensions to the scholarship on China as a growing economic power and will be of particular interest to international economists, political scientists, and business scholars studying China. Jun Fu is Associate Professor in the School of Economics and Management, Tsinghua University.

narrative:
Short impact summary

Institutions and Investments has a clear scholarly footprint: OpenAlex records 43 citations, placing it in the top 10% of works in its field and year. Its citation pattern shows sustained use in research on foreign direct investment, China’s institutional reforms, and regional development, with most uptake appearing in academic journals and edited volumes.

Full narrative

Published by the University of Michigan Press in 2000, Institutions and Investments has become a recognized reference for scholarship on how institutional change shapes foreign direct investment in China. The book’s citation record indicates durable academic relevance over time rather than a short-lived burst of attention. Its strongest reuse appears in work on international business and FDI, global political economy, and China’s socioeconomic governance, which aligns closely with the book’s interdisciplinary framing across economics, law, business, and political science.

The citing literature is concentrated in scholarly venues, especially journal articles and book chapters, and includes recent work as well as earlier follow-on studies. This suggests that the book continues to inform research questions about investment behavior, policy design, and the institutional conditions that shape capital flows. The record also shows substantial use within education-sector research, with citations coming largely from academic institutions and a wide range of countries, including the United States, China, and Taiwan.

The book’s influence is also visible in the thematic range of citing works. Recent citations connect it to studies of informal political coalitions, factional politics and FDI, border economic zones, and industry-level investment localization in China. That pattern points to a broad afterlife for the book’s core argument: institutional and political arrangements remain central to understanding where foreign investment goes and how it behaves.

Beyond citation evidence, the work shows some signs of broader relevance. It is associated with the SDG theme Partnerships for the goals, reflecting policy-facing interest in institutional cooperation and development. Library holdings and subject classifications also indicate continuing discoverability in collections focused on foreign investment and China’s economic conditions. At the same time, the public-discourse record is limited in the sources available here, so the most reliable evidence of impact remains its sustained scholarly uptake.
